comments:
Here a few thoughts:

What is for me important is the quality of the submission, regardless of human or AI generated. This means: the contribution should be adequately justified (just because an AI can write a lot of code, it does not mean that any contribution makes sense; there need to be strict filtering criteria on what is considered a helpful contribution and what just pure code spamming), should be adequately documented in the description and code-comments, and the code should be clean (avoid avalanche of code; understand and respect the eco-system of functions in a codebase, etc). It turns out that as of today, AI generated contributions without humans in the loop are by far not reaching the quality standard, yet. 

Until open-source projects are maintained by humans, any contribution to these projects need to be tailored such that it is digestible by a human maintainer. If in the future there will be a proliferation of open source projects maintained mostly by agents, I think we could change many of the rules for the contributions, in particular, it is no longer as compelling that the description of a contribution is written in a clean prose accessible to humans; even terse and verbose prose could be considered as acceptable.

Good luck!
Andrea

comments:
In reality, I spend more time developing my own projects, and I often see people showing up with code generated using AI.

Very often, people simply give a task to an AI agent and do not even look at the resulting code - they only check whether it works. The agent does not even try to produce code that follows the project's standards. It frequently makes highly questionable decisions that look more like hacks than the intended behavior.

Working with such contributors becomes very difficult because I maintain my projects alone, and I do not have enough free time after work to explain to every person what is wrong with their code.

I even had an experience where I started communicating with such a contributor and helping improve their pull request. They would simply pass my comments to the AI agent and then submit another batch of strange code. Eventually, it got to the point where I just said: "Delete everything you did here and paste in this code that I wrote."

I eventually made it a rule that if a pull request was created with the help of AI, I will not review it and will close it immediately.

I think it mostly comes down to how invested the author is in their project. For me, it is much more important to understand the code and keep it clean than to add a bunch of strange features through AI. A friend of mine, on the other hand, created a project where all code is added exclusively through AI. He does not really understand any of it himself, and if his AI agent were taken away, he would not be able to maintain the project for very long until he learned how it actually works.
